title: Controlling eutrophication by combined bloom precipitation and sediment phosphorus inactivation
organism: Aphanizomenon flos-aquae (lake); Microcystis aeruginosa scum from pond De Ploeg (lab)
scale: Lab: 18 tubes of 100 mL, triplicates; whole lake: Lake Rauwbraken (NL), 4 ha, max depth 15 m, stratifying, groundwater-fed with no in/outflow
dose: Lab: PAC 0, 2.2, 4.4 mg Al/L with or without 390 mg/L La-modified bentonite; lake: 2 t PAC + 18 t Phoslock over 21-23 April 2008
duration: Lab 2 h; lake monitored April 2008 through 2013
result: 'Floc and Lock' sank the bloom; mean chlorophyll-a fell from 19.5 to 3.7 ug/L and TP from 169 to 14 ug/L, keeping the lake oligo-mesotrophic through 2013.
env_effects: Adds aluminium and lanthanum clay permanently to the sediment; in the lab neither PAC nor Phoslock alone sank buoyant Microcystis.
key_details: Lab test on Microcystis scum (~845 µg chl-a/L): after 2 h, PAC alone at 2.2 mg Al/L and LMB alone did not sink the buoyant cells (4.4 mg Al/L helped somewhat), but PAC + LMB together moved chlorophyll to the tube bottoms (significant PAC, LMB and interaction effects). Whole-lake 'Flock & Lock' in April 2008 sank a developing Aphanizomenon bloom; mean chl-a fell from 19.5 (±36.5) µg/L in the two years before to 3.7 (±4.5) µg/L after, and TP from 169 (±126) to 14 (±15) µg/L. The lake stayed oligo-mesotrophic through 2013. Single small, isolated, groundwater-fed lake with no control lake; the lake had a 4-month swimming ban in 2007.

title: Management of eutrophication in Lake De Kuil (The Netherlands) using combined flocculant – Lanthanum modified bentonite treatment
authors: Guido Waajen, Frank Van Oosterhout, Grant Douglas, Miquel Lürling
scale: Whole lake, Lake De Kuil (NL): 6.7 ha, mean depth 4 m, max 9 m, 268,000 m³, residence time 3.7 y
dose: 4.38 t FeCl3 (3 m³) over 6.7 ha, buffered with 200 kg Ca(OH)2; LMB 13.65 t spread over 6.7 ha plus 27.85 t injected over 2.2 ha deeper than 6.4 m; May 2009
result: Mean summer chlorophyll-a fell from 16 to 6 ug/L and TP from 0.05 to 0.02 mg/L; bathing standards were met for six summers and macrophyte cover tripled.
env_effects: Secchi rose from 1.5 m to 5 m immediately after treatment; macrophyte cover tripled 2009-2011. Sediment P release fell from 5.2 (2009) to 0.4 mg P/m²/d (2010) but increased in later years, risking reversion.
key_details: Before-after whole-lake study with long-term monitoring (1992-2008 vs 2009-2014), no reference lake. Iron(III) chloride was used instead of PAC because an aluminium permit was refused. Mean summer TP fell from 0.05 to 0.02 mg/L, chlorophyll a from 16 to 6 µg/L and Secchi rose from 2.31 to 3.12 m; bathing-water requirements were met six summers in a row. A Planktothrix rubescens bloom occurred in winter 2010/2011, but summer cyanobacteria biomass was lower than before treatment. Success relied on external P loading being near the critical load; rising sediment P release in later years limits longevity.

title: Eutrophication management in surface waters using lanthanum modified bentonite: A review
authors: Diego Copetti, Karin Finsterle, Laura Marziali, Fabrizio Stefani, Gianni Tartari, Grant Douglas et al.
scale: ~200 treated water bodies worldwide; lab, mesocosm and whole-lake
result: LMB strongly binds phosphate (SRP cut >98% in 7-d core batch tests and 87-98% in 48-h water tests). Field and mesocosm results vary: e.g. Lake Varese mesocosm bottom-water TP 0.11 → 0.04 mg/L, but one 58-day trial showed treated TP (median 0.58 mg/L) not substantially different from control (0.69 mg/L). Efficacy is reduced by humic substances and pH > 9.
env_effects: La generally below acute toxicity thresholds except in low-alkalinity waters; La accumulation, suspended solids and effects on sediment organisms unresolved; use in saline waters needs careful risk evaluation (La release).
key_details: Narrative review (author accepted manuscript) of LMB/Phoslock in ~200 water bodies. Lab batch tests showed >98% SRP reduction in 7 days and 87-98% in 48 h. Mesocosms gave 94-100% SRP and 83-96% TP reductions over up to 73 days. Field outcomes varied: the Lake Varese mesocosm showed >80% TP/SRP reduction vs the untreated site over 11 months, but another 58-day study found no substantial TP difference from controls. Direct cyanobacteria or chlorophyll outcomes are reported only sparsely, e.g. no scums or algaecide needed in one lake in 2013. Much of the evidence is industry grey literature.

title: Longevity and effectiveness of aluminum addition to reduce sediment phosphorus release and restore lake water quality
authors: Brian Huser, Sara Egemose, Harvey H. Harper, Michael Hupfer, Henning Skovgaard Jensen, Keith M. Pilgrim et al.
result: Across 114 Al-treated lakes, short-term epilimnetic TP fell from 0.101 to 0.036 mg/L and chl-a from 42.7 to 16.3 µg/L, with Secchi rising 1.6 → 2.4 m. TP-based longevity averaged 11 years (Secchi 9.7 and chl-a 8.8 years); stratified lakes lasted longer than polymictic ones, and Al dose explained 47% of longevity variation.
env_effects: Adds aluminium to sediments; benthic-feeding fish in shallow lakes appear to shorten effectiveness.
key_details: Multi-lake synthesis of 114 lakes (Denmark, Germany, Sweden, US) treated with Al salts, comparing ≥2 years of pre-treatment growing-season data with post-treatment data. Longevity was defined as years with ≥50% improvement in TP or chl-a, or a Secchi increase. Paired tests: TP 0.101 → 0.036 mg/L, chl-a 42.7 → 16.3 µg/L (~62% lower), Secchi 1.6 → 2.4 m. Longevity averaged 11 years for TP (15 using modelled values) and 8.8 years for chl-a. Stratified lakes averaged 15 years observed (21 modelled) vs 4.6-5.7 years for polymictic lakes. Dose, watershed:lake area and Osgood index explained 47%, 32% and 3% of longevity variance. There were no untreated control lakes.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record gave no algal outcome (effect_pct null). The full text reports the chl-a drop of 42.7 → 16.3 µg/L (~62%) and a chl-a longevity of 8.8 years.

title: A meta-analysis of water quality and aquatic macrophyte responses in 18 lakes treated with lanthanum modified bentonite (Phoslock®)
authors: Bryan M. Spears, Eleanor B. Mackay, Said Yasseri, Iain Gunn, Kate E. Waters, Christopher Andrews et al.
result: Median TP fell 0.08 → 0.03 mg/L and SRP 0.019 → 0.005 mg/L in the 24 months after La-bentonite. Median annual chl-a barely changed (10.1 → 10.0 µg/L; the drop was significant only in Z-scores), spring chl-a fell 14.0 → 6.2 µg/L, and the summer 75th percentile fell 119 → 74 µg/L.
env_effects: Macrophyte recovery and clarity improved; responses highly site-specific.
key_details: Before-after meta-analysis of 18 lakes treated with La-bentonite (1.4-6.7 t/ha), comparing the 24 months before and after first application. There were no untreated control lakes: TP, chl-a and Secchi data came from 15 lakes, SRP from 14, macrophyte species from 6 and colonisation depth from 4. TP and SRP fell significantly. Median annual chl-a was essentially unchanged (10.1 → 10.0 µg/L), with the largest relative response in spring (14.0 → 6.2 µg/L). The 75th-percentile shifts (summer chl-a 119 → 74 µg/L, Secchi 398 → 506 cm) were not formally tested. Macrophyte species rose from a median of 5.5 to 7.0.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record's effect_pct of 37.8 came from the summer 75th-percentile chl-a (119 → 74 µg/L), which the paper says was not tested statistically. The median annual chl-a change was only 10.1 → 10.0 µg/L (~1%), significant only after Z-score transformation, so the record overstates the algal response.

title: Lake responses following lanthanum-modified bentonite clay (Phoslock®) application: An analysis of water column lanthanum data from 16 case study lakes
authors: Bryan M. Spears, Miquel Lürling, Said Yasseri, Ana Teresa Castro, Max M. Gibbs, Sebastian Meis et al.
result: Post-application surface total La peaked at 0.026-2.30 mg/L and filterable La at 0.002-0.14 mg/L, returning toward baseline in 3-12 months.
env_effects: Surface filterable La exceeded the Ceriodaphnia dubia EC50 (0.08 mg/L) in Loch Flemington during application and in a Niedersachsen lake for 2 months afterwards, falling to 0.001-0.002 mg/L by month 6. In at least two lakes FLa never returned below the <0.001 mg/L baseline during monitoring. Modelled La³⁺ was <0.0004 mg/L at alkalinity >0.8 mEq/L but up to 0.12 mg/L in very low-alkalinity lakes.
key_details: Analysis of water-column lanthanum in 16 lakes treated with Phoslock, monitored up to 60 months after application; pre-application TLa and FLa were <0.001 mg/L everywhere. Maximum post-application surface TLa was 0.026-2.30 mg/L and FLa 0.002-0.14 mg/L. Generalised additive models showed 2nd-order decay, reaching an end-point 3-12 months after application. Product concentrations as suspended solids (0.62-46.0 mg/L) stayed below lab EC50s (e.g. Daphnia 871 mg/L). This is a safety/exposure paper with no algal-response data.
fulltext_discrepancy: The record left out that FLa exceeded the C. dubia EC50 (0.08 mg/L) in two lakes and did not return to baseline in at least two lakes.

title: Humic substances interfere with phosphate removal by lanthanum modified clay in controlling eutrophication
authors: Miquel Lürling, Guido Waajen, Frank Van Oosterhout
dose: Phoslock 50 mg/L (4.37% La measured by ICP-MS) with ~0.6 mg/L FRP and humic substances 0-14 mg/L DOC
result: Humic substances lowered Phoslock's FRP removal in both the 1-d and 42-d experiments, matching equilibrium modelling; even without DOC, 24-h FRP removal was only 46% and 42-d residual FRP was ~34% higher than predicted. Filterable La rose above 270 µg/L within a week with humics, vs the Dutch standard of 10.1 µg/L.
env_effects: Filterable lanthanum exceeded 270 µg/L in the presence of humic substances, far above the Dutch surface-water La standard of 10.1 µg/L.
key_details: Controlled lab experiments plus CHEAQS/WHAM chemical equilibrium modelling of La-humic complexation at pH 7 and 8. Short-term (24 h) series compared FRP solutions with and without 50 mg/L Phoslock across eight DOC levels (0-14 mg/L); a 42-day experiment followed. Modelling predicted only 81.7% of P could bind as LaPO4 at the dose used, and DOC reduced this further. Authors conclude the recommended Phoslock dose seems too low and DOC-rich waters need site-specific testing. No algae were measured; FRP of 600 µg/L is higher than typical field values.

title: Effects of alum treatment on water quality and sediment in the Minneapolis Chain of Lakes, Minnesota, USA
authors: Brian Huser, Patrick L. Brezonik, Raymond M. Newman
scale: 4 lakes, Minneapolis Chain of Lakes (MN, USA)
result: Growing-season chl-a fell from 12.2 to 3.7 µg/L (Calhoun), 7.2 to 4.1 (Harriet), 15.5 to 4.9 (Cedar, 5 yr post) and 35.3 to 17.4 (Isles, 5 yr post); Lake of the Isles (lowest dose) returned to pretreatment levels by 2002-2005, while internal P release still stayed suppressed in all four lakes.
env_effects: Alum floc drifted to deeper sediments; adds aluminium.
key_details: Before-after field evaluation of alum treatments in four Minneapolis lakes (Cedar and Isles 1996; Harriet, littoral-only, and Calhoun 2001) using biweekly monitoring since 1991, with no untreated reference lake. Secchi depth rose significantly in all lakes (e.g. Calhoun 2.7 to 4.7 m). Internal P release fell from 9.7 to 1.3 mg/m²/d in Cedar (rising to 4.8 in 2002-2003), from 10.6 to 1.6 mg/m²/d in Harriet (85%), was nearly eliminated in Calhoun, and fell from 5.9 to 1.7 mg/m²/d in Isles. In Harriet the floc drifted to deeper sediments, giving unexpected improvement. Isles' TP and chl-a in 2002-2005 were not significantly different from pretreatment despite lower sediment release, pointing to external loading.

title: Impact of iron addition on phosphorus dynamics in sediments of a shallow peat lake 10 years after treatment
authors: Melanie Münch, Rianne van Kaam, Karel As, Stefan Peiffer, Gerard ter Heerdt, Caroline P. Slomp et al.
scale: Whole shallow peat lake Terra Nova (NL)
dose: 40% FeCl3 solution applied continuously at low doses over 1.5 years from 2010; total 0.5-1 mol Fe/m² (1 mol Fe/m² in the test area)
duration: Treatment 1.5 years (2010-2011); sediment study ~10 years later (2021)
result: Surface-water TP stayed below 0.5 µmol/L for ~1.5 years after treatment. Afterwards summer internal P loading returned stronger (whole-lake anoxic flux ~505 µmol P m⁻² d⁻¹; in situ ~420), producing the highest surface-water P since monitoring began in 1986.
env_effects: Organic-rich sediment released P in excess of Fe under summer low oxygen; the treatment backfired long-term.
key_details: Single-lake case study (Terra Nova, NL; shallow peat lake with filamentous cyanobacteria blooms 1987-2004) about 10 years after FeCl3 dosing. There was no control lake; the design is long-term monitoring plus sediment cores from 3 stations incubated oxic and anoxic for 26 days. Sediment released 10-84× more P under anoxic than oxic conditions. The added Fe still redox-cycles in the top 10 cm and binds up to 70% of sedimentary P, but organic matter keeps Fe²⁺ in the solid phase and limits re-capture. The authors could not fully explain why suppression lasted only 1.5 years.
fulltext_discrepancy: The treatment was a continuous low-dose application over 1.5 years, not a single dose, and P suppression lasted ~1.5 years; the record's 'two years' follows the abstract. The post-treatment P peak was the highest since 1986.

title: The effect of alum coagulation for in-lake treatment of toxic Microcystis and other cyanobacteria related organisms in microcosm experiments
authors: Jisun Han, Bong-Seok Jeon, Noriko Futatsugi, Ho-Dong Park
organism: Microcystis ichthyoblabe strain TAC95 (produces only microcystin-LR); sediment bacteria
scale: 3 acrylic microcosm chambers (5 L Microcystis suspension each; +sediment, +alum, +alum+sediment) plus bottle experiments
dose: Alum at the maximum dose keeping pH 6.0: 48 mg/L as Al (microcosm) and 35 mg/L as Al (bottles)
result: Alum co-precipitated the cells so chlorophyll-a and intracellular MC-LR in the water fell sharply within 1 day, but in the +alum microcosm >95% of intracellular MC-LR was released to the water by day 7. With sediment present, extracellular MC-LR rose for 3 days and then fell.
env_effects: Harmed cyanobacteria-lysing organisms and microcystin-degrading bacteria; authors conclude alum at this dose is unsuitable for bloom removal without toxin release.
key_details: Lab microcosms (320 x 180 x 150 mm chambers) with washed M. ichthyoblabe in dechlorinated tap water; one chamber per treatment (+sediment control, +alum, +alum+sediment), with sediment from a eutrophic pond. Alum was dosed at the jar-test maximum that keeps pH at 6.0. No Microcystis-lysing bacterial plaques appeared in the +alum microcosm, and plaque counts in +alum+sediment were far lower than in +sediment alone; alum also reduced microcystin-degrading bacterial activity. Chlorophyll-a and phycocyanin fell in the precipitated cells. The authors conclude alum is not suitable for removing toxic blooms because floc remains in sediment for a long time. Caveat: very high dose and apparently a single chamber per treatment.
fulltext_discrepancy: The organism is Microcystis ichthyoblabe (TAC95), not M. aeruginosa; the setting is indoor lab microcosms (5 L chambers), not a mesocosm. The record omits that alum first removed chlorophyll-a from the water column by co-precipitation within 1 day.

title: Trophic state decrease after lanthanum-modified bentonite (Phoslock) application to a hyper-eutrophic polymictic urban lake frequented by Canada geese (Branta canadensis)
authors: Gertrud K. Nürnberg, Bruce D. LaZerte
scale: Whole lake, Swan Lake (Greater Toronto), 5.5 ha, max depth 4.4 m, polymictic former gravel pit, terminal lake with limited flushing
dose: Phoslock (La-modified bentonite) 25.2 metric tonnes, 4.6 t/ha, applied 29 April-1 May 2013
duration: Pre-treatment monitoring from August 2011; 2 years post-treatment (2013-2014)
result: Mean TP fell from 0.247 to 0.099 mg/L (year 1) and 0.060 mg/L (year 2); phytoplankton biomass fell only in year 2, when growing-season Secchi rose to 1.4 m from 0.5 m, moving the lake from hyper-eutrophic to eutrophic. Canada geese then supplied ~75% of nutrient input.
env_effects: Waterfowl (geese) supplied ~75% of nutrients; repeated treatment or waterfowl management recommended.
key_details: Before-after study of a single hyper-eutrophic urban lake without a control lake; phytoplankton tracked as chlorophyll a (uncorrected) and Secchi depth. First-year TP and TN fell 60% and 40% but trophic state did not change, attributed to late application after winter sediment P had already been taken up by phytoplankton. Mixing regime (Schmidt stability 1-6 J/m²) was similar before and after, so changes were not due to mixing. Pre-treatment internal load was estimated at 650-1100 mg/m²/yr; hypoxia remained widespread. Authors recommend goose management or repeat treatment.

title: In situ evaluation of options for chemical treatment of hepatotoxic cyanobacterial blooms
authors: Angeline K.-Y. Lam, Ellie E. Prepas
venue: Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences
scale: Closed-bottom limnocorrals in a hardwater Alberta lake
dose: Lime-alum vs Reglone A algicide vs lime alone
result: Lime-alum and Reglone A both removed phytoplankton, but exo-microcystin in lime-alum enclosures peaked 32-fold lower than with the lytic algicide.
env_effects: Lime alone raised pH above 10 and increased dissolved microcystin (pH shock); lime-alum precipitated intact cells without toxin release.
